Gradient Boosting with a SHAP Distance for Case-Based Reasoning

Source: R/boost.R
BoostModel.Rd

Gradient Boosting with a SHAP Distance for Case-Based Reasoning

Gradient Boosting with a SHAP Distance for Case-Based Reasoning

Details

Fits a gradient-boosted tree model with xgboost and measures the distance between two cases in the space of their SHAP values (Lundberg et al., 2020). With \(\phi_k(x)\) the SHAP value of variable \(k\), i.e. its contribution to the prediction of case \(x\) on the margin scale of the model (outcome, log odds or log relative hazard), $$d(x_i, x_j) = \sum_k |\phi_k(x_i) - \phi_k(x_j)|.$$ This is the contribution-space distance of the regression models with the variables as terms: for a linear model, \(\phi_k(x) = \beta_k (x_k - \bar x_k)\), and the distance is the weighted distance of Dippon et al. (2002). Because the SHAP values add up to the model's prediction, the distance bounds the difference of the predictions on the margin scale; for the Cox objective, \(e^{d}\) bounds the hazard ratio of the two cases.

The endpoint determines the objective: Surv(time, status) uses "survival:cox", two classes (factor, character, logical or 0/1) "binary:logistic", more classes "multi:softprob" (the SHAP values of all classes are used), and numeric endpoints "reg:squarederror". Only the variables of the formula are used, not transformations or interactions: the trees find non-linear effects and interactions themselves. Unordered factors are one-hot encoded and their SHAP values summed per variable; ordered factors are used as their ranks.

Every split of the model is part of the distance: choose nrounds and max_depth by cross-validation (xgboost::xgb.cv() with early stopping) rather than by default, otherwise splits in irrelevant features become distance. The Methods vignette shows how.

Without row or column subsampling (the default), the model and the distance are deterministic. New cases (add_cases()) need no refit: their SHAP values are computed with the fitted model.

References

Lundberg, S. M. et al. (2020). From local explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees. Nature Machine Intelligence, 2, 56–67. doi:10.1038/s42256-019-0138-9

Chen, T. and Guestrin, C. (2016). XGBoost: A scalable tree boosting system. Proceedings of KDD 2016, 785–794. doi:10.1145/2939672.2939785

Method new()

Initialize a gradient boosting model for searching similar cases.

Usage

BoostModel$new(
  formula,
  data,
  nrounds = 100,
  params = list(eta = 0.1, max_depth = 3)
)

Arguments

formula

Object of class formula or character, e.g. y ~ x1 + x2 or Surv(time, status) ~ ..

data

Training data of class data.frame

nrounds

number of boosting rounds

params

list of xgboost parameters, e.g. eta, max_depth, lambda; objective is set from the endpoint unless given.

Method shap_values()

SHAP values of cases: one column per variable (for multi-class models, per variable and class), on the margin scale of the model.

Usage

BoostModel$shap_values(data)

Arguments

data

data.frame with the variables of the model

Returns

A matrix with attribute bias (the expected margin).

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("xgboost", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(survival)
  lung2 <- na.omit(lung[, c("time", "status", "age", "sex", "ph.ecog")])
  lung2$status <- lung2$status - 1
  m <- BoostModel$new(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, lung2, nrounds = 50)
  m$fit()
  m$get_similar_cases(lung2[1:2, ], k = 3)
  m$explain_match(lung2[1, ], lung2[2, ])
}
